>   
> First of all, let me express my deep appreciation for the work you have been doing over the past years. Truly, I must say that the way you present your understanding of the world, and how events have evolved throughout history from a different perspective, is both amazing and eye-opening.

Perhaps this is also why you choose to use a board rather than simply speaking into a microphone behind a desk—it greatly enhances understanding.  
>   
> I have also found your interviews with a wide range of interviewers very engaging. You mentioned a few times that you used to play StarCraft, which I also played extensively. >   
> However, to turn to a more serious matter and my main question:  
>   
> Given the current turbulent developments in the world, which may have a significant impact on large parts of the population, I sometimes find myself feeling anxious after watching your videos and listening to your messages. >

> Professor Jiang, you asked us to find holes in your logic. I went through all 133 of your lectures systematically. Here are 5 questions I can't resolve:

> 1. Your framework is unfalsifiable — and you know it.  
>   
> In Geo-Strategy END, you said psychohistory can model and predict history. In GT #18, you argue Trump is "deliberately losing" the Iran war. But this is unfalsifiable: if the US wins, Trump is a genius. If the US loses, Trump is ALSO a genius (because he wanted to lose). If neither happens, "it's not time yet." In Geo-Strategy #11, you predict civil war in "10 to 50 years" — a window so wide it can never be proven wrong. Karl Popper would call this pseudoscience: a framework that can explain any outcome predicts nothing.  
>   
> So my question: *What specific outcome, if it happened, would prove your framework wrong?* Not "I'll adjust the model" — what would BREAK it?  
>   
> 2. Your biggest specific prediction was wrong, and it broke your causal chain.  
>   
> In Geo-Strategy #5, your central argument was that Trump would pick Nikki Haley as VP, and she would be the one to push for the Iran war. Trump picked JD Vance. This wasn't a minor detail — it was the ENGINE of your Iran prediction. The cause you identified (Haley's hawkish agenda + VP platform) didn't happen, yet the effect you predicted (Iran war) may have happened anyway. If the same outcome occurs through a completely different mechanism than the one you predicted, doesn't that mean your model identified a false cause? You predicted the right destination but drew the wrong map.  
>   
> 3. You hold two "ultimate truths" that contradict each other.  
>   
> In Secret History and Game Theory, your operating assumption is that the fundamental driver of human behavior is STATUS COMPETITION — everything is a zero-sum game for power positions. But in Great Books #6 and #7, you argue that the deepest insight of Homer, Virgil, and the great poets is that LOVE is the fundamental law of the universe, and the pursuit of power is a violation of that law. Both claims use the word "fundamental." If status competition is the root of everything, then love is just a byproduct. If love is the fundamental law, then status competition is a pathology, not a foundation. Which is it? You can't have two different "bottom layers."  
>   
> 4. Elite overproduction explains everything, therefore it explains nothing.  
>   
> You use elite overproduction to explain: the Bronze Age Collapse, Maya collapse, the fall of Rome, the French Revolution, the Peloponnesian War, the 2008 financial crisis, and American polarization. When one theory explains EVERY collapse in human history, it has lost all discriminating power. More importantly: where are the counterexamples? Victorian Britain had massive elite surplus (younger sons of aristocrats with no inheritance) — they were channeled to colonies, and Britain thrived. Song Dynasty China had enormous numbers of failed exam candidates — yet Song didn't collapse from internal revolution, it fell to external Mongol invasion. Peter Turchin himself never claimed elite overproduction was the ONLY cause — he uses it as one variable in a four-variable quantitative model. You stripped away the math and kept only the slogan.  
>

>   
> You've said: "Schools are designed to brainwash" (SH #1), "Schools are designed to control, not educate" (Civ #54), "Schools teach you not to explore" (Civ #35). This teacher earns genuine respect rather than mere compliance.

A man secure enough in his knowledge to invite challenge, to say "test this, break it if you can", has nothing to prove and nothing to hide. He is not building followers; he is building thinkers.
That is the mark of true intellectual courage.

The teacher who demands unquestioning agreement is, at some level, afraid.. afraid his ideas cannot survive scrutiny, afraid his authority depends on silence rather than substance. On the contrary the one who hands his students a torch and says "go find the holes in what I've told you" trusts both the truth and the people in the room. There is something noble in it - he is verily subordinating his ego to the pursuit of something larger. He knows that if his teaching is sound, it will hold up. and if it doesn't, he would rather know.

This kind of teacher leaves a different mark.. his students don't just carry his lessons; they carry the habit of questioning, which is far more durable and far more valuable. He multiplies his impact not by creating dependents, but by sending out minds that can stand on their own.

This teacher stands apart in a world full of people who mistake certainty for strength. He understands that real authority is earned through openness, not guarded through blind obedience.

PART 1 of 3
I always appreciate your lectures and am genuinely excited to listen to each one. The way you connect geopolitics, economics, history, and eschatology into a single coherent framework is something I have never encountered anywhere else, and it has fundamentally changed the way I see the world. That said, putting my admiration aside, and given the spirit of the midterm assignment in which you invited us to challenge your logic as rigorously as possible, I would like to raise the following counterarguments. I do so not out of disagreement for its own sake, but out of the deepest respect for the critical thinking methodology you have taught us.
Question 1: The Oil Supply Substitution Argument and the Possibility of Energy Transition
In Game Theory #18 Trump World Order, you argue: "This war will knock out the Middle Eastern producers, leaving Venezuela, Canada, and the United States. North America and Russia. This means Asia and Europe will now become dependent on North American energy and fertilizer exports, and America stands to benefit in the long run."
Yet in The Hollywood-Pentagon Complex, you also predict: "If oil prices skyrocket, civilian aviation will collapse, fertilizer shortages will make it impossible to feed 8 billion people, and global famine will follow. This will bring about deindustrialization and the collapse of urban populations."
I believe there is a genuine logical tension between these two claims. If North America and Russia function as replacement suppliers, nations around the world should be able to resolve the oil shortage simply by shifting their imports away from the Middle East. The absolute quantity of oil on the planet does not disappear. You yourself stated that "Canada has enormous oil reserves" and that "Venezuela holds the world's largest reserves." If that is the case, why would the oil shortage cause deindustrialization so severe that it constitutes civilizational collapse? Or is your scenario not actually about an absolute scarcity of oil, but rather about the soaring costs of transition and geopolitical control over supply chains? If so, isn't that a fundamentally different problem — not "civilizational collapse due to oil scarcity," but rather "a redistribution of wealth through the restructuring of energy hegemony"?
Furthermore, in The Return of History, you make no mention of alternative energy sources. Yet many advanced economies — particularly Japan, France, and South Korea — rely heavily on nuclear power, and coal, LNG, and renewables are already embedded in existing energy mixes. Your deindustrialization scenario appears to rest on the implicit assumption that no substitutes for oil exist. This is especially puzzling given that in The Return of History you suggest Japan has a reasonable chance of survival — yet Japan is one of the most oil-dependent nations in the developed world. On what basis do you believe Japan can survive within the logic of your own framework?

> Question 2: China's Sea Lane Blockade and the Dilemma of Forced Escalation  
> In The Hollywood-Pentagon Complex, you state that America intends to dominate four major chokepoints — the Panama Canal, the Middle East, the Strait of Malacca, and Greenland — to place conditions on China's access to trade. In The Law of Asymmetry, you argue that "China will triangulate between Russia and America and attempt to maintain neutrality." Yet in The Return of History, you state that "if BRICS — Russia, Iran, and China — unite, that constitutes the consolidation of the Heartland, and America must prevent this at all costs."  
> I believe there is a fundamental contradiction here. On one hand, you argue that China will maintain indifference and not directly confront America. On the other hand, you suggest that if America blocks China's sea lanes, China will deindustrialize. These two propositions cannot logically coexist.  
> Approximately 20% of China's GDP depends on exports, and its industrial production is sustained by energy imports. If America effectively cuts off China's oil supply through the Strait of Malacca and the Strait of Hormuz, China's economy would suffer catastrophic damage within months — fundamentally destroying the CCP's legitimacy, which rests on maintaining economic growth. Under these circumstances, is it politically feasible for China's leadership to continue declaring "this has nothing to do with us"? Given that Mao Zedong built the CCP's legitimacy on "the people's resistance against imperialist aggression," wouldn't a sea lane blockade constitute an act tantamount to a declaration of war?  
> Your framework contains an inescapable dilemma. If America enforces a thorough sea lane blockade, China faces economic collapse and is compelled to take military action — China goes to war. If America does not enforce the blockade thoroughly, China continues to support Iran through BRICS and America's Heartland strategy fails — America loses. Under either scenario, the equilibrium state you describe — "China maintains neutrality while America and China coexist" — appears unattainable.

### **@kennethbrantley1984** | 👍 3 likes

Hi Prof Jiang - here is my midterm, if I’m not too late! 

1a. The Torah as Davidic propaganda? 

If David invented the Torah to consolidate power, it seems he was appealing to Scripture as it already existed — invoking the authority of Abraham, Moses, the patriarchs. The propaganda theory requires a prior authority to borrow legitimacy from. You cannot bootstrap sacred authority from nothing. The theory seems to eat itself - why would unconnected groups of nomads, Egyptian priests, hill people, and mercenaries be willing to submit to circumcision, animal sacrifice, dietary law? Why would they have any reason to believe in the legitimacy of what this mercenary king created? 

1b. Paul as a Roman spy

Why did Rome need Paul? Rome had armies. If the ministry of Jesus resulted in civil unrest of the lower class, why would Rome suddenly pivot from its notorious use of brutal violence? What Rome consistently did with early Christians was feed them to lions, which is a strange way to manage your own propaganda apparatus. The execution of Paul himself is pretty well attested for historically - at least as much as is the crucifixion of Jesus. Why would he die for what he knew to be manufactured? Isn’t a more reasonable explanation that, as the message of Jesus spread over the decades, the upper class of the collapsing Roman Empire inserted self serving mechanisms (Greek mystery religions, alignment with Roman patriarchy system) to co-opt increasingly popular institution? 

1c. The self-fulfilling prophecy problem

The eschatological convergence framework derives its predictive power from these traditions. Essentially, it posits that even if the traditions are false, they function as self-fulfilling prophecies, and tracking their eschatological convergence helps predict real outcomes. However - we know that successful propaganda serves the interests of those who produce it, and when we look at the actual conditions/motivations of the parties involved:
-David had every incentive to present himself as the fulfillment of existing covenant promises — not to invent new ones that constrained his own power. The Torah’s Law is remarkably inconvenient for a king — it explicitly limits royal power, prohibits the accumulation of horses and wives and gold, and makes the king subject to the same Law as everyone else. Why would a propaganda-writing mercenary king design such a thing?
-Paul had every incentive to accommodate Roman power if he were its agent — instead he was executed by it. Paul’s teaching should have been incentivized to remove the crucifixion from their central story if they were designing propaganda for a Roman audience — a crucified Messiah was, as Paul himself acknowledged, a stumbling block to Jews and foolishness to Greeks. Why design a message around the thing most likely to make their audience reject it?

1d. My final question

I can’t figure out how, if these traditions are self-fulfilling prophecies whose value lies in their institutional success, what accounts for the pre-dated texts?

Isaiah 53 is a famous example of this - confirmed by Dead Sea Scrolls copies that predate Jesus by at least a century, it describes in specific narrative detail a figure whose hands and feet were pierced, who was silent before his accusers, buried with the rich, and survived his own death - and was written before crucifixion existed as a method of execution. How is this accounted for, other than what the text itself claims?

Another example, though more speculative than Isaiah 53, is Revelation 13. It seems to describe something very similar to the systems of control and oppression that you also have predicted with your framework, which establishes control over the world’s market and currency system - despite being written nearly two millennia ago. 

Self-fulfilling prophecy requires the prophecy to be known and then enacted. These were not enacted by people who set out to fulfill them — they were enacted by people who were, in most cases, trying to stop them.

If the traditions are merely successful propaganda whose institutional momentum produces convergent predictions, what produced the pre-dated texts that no editing or amount of self-fulfillment could seem to have arranged?

In the spirit of Occam’s razor, is it not a much more simple explanation that eschatological convergence works because, among the eschatologies, there is something of actual veracity?

Dear Professor,


I would like to express my sincere gratitude for your lectures on geopolitics and game theory that you have delivered and shared on YouTube over time. Those video lectures have profoundly helped me perceive the world from a multidimensional perspective. They have taught me how to trace every issue from its very roots to its ultimate consequences—a systematic and well-structured method of thinking. I truly appreciate them, and in fact, the philosophies conveyed in your lectures perfectly align with the profound questions I have harbored for so long.


Recently, while observing global geopolitical shifts—from the rise and the bottlenecks of superpowers like China to the fierce technological race with the West—I found myself drawn into a stream of thought that goes far beyond surface-level news. It has led me to a profound skepticism regarding the very structure of human society. I deeply yearn to hear your wise perspective on this matter.


I know my rote memory may not be flawless, but I am fairly confident in my ability to synthesize information and grasp the fundamental lessons. Therefore, when referencing your lectures, I might express the underlying essence as I understood it rather than quoting you verbatim. I hope for your understanding in this regard.


The story begins with my realization of a rather bitter truth: Millions of diligent engineers working tirelessly to optimize technology cannot shift the global paradigm as effectively as a small group of genius scientists who hold the "core technology."


This is not merely a subjective feeling, but a validated reality; the aforementioned scenario is just one of the countless manifestations of this root issue. In terms of universal principles, Price’s Law of creative productivity reveals a harsh truth: in any given domain involving millions, 50% of the greatest breakthroughs are always produced by a tiny minority equal to the square root of the total population. Looking at the physical and geopolitical realities of today, millions of engineers, armed with a relentless work ethic and hundreds of billions of dollars in state funding from Eastern superpowers, remain powerless before the barrier of EUV lithography—a core technology held by an incredibly small group of brilliant Western minds at ASML.


This irony, much like what Harvard Professor Michael Sandel calls "The Tyranny of Merit," shatters humanity's most universal and naive belief: "Just try your best and you will win." It exposes humanity's "original injustice": mechanical effort and collective strength are sometimes completely subdued by the asymmetrical superiority of minds that inherited exceptional genetics and elite circumstances.


From that initial fracture, I began to look more broadly at the structure of society. If nature is inherently unjust, then isn't the concept of "absolute fairness" or "common prosperity" touted by regimes worldwide essentially just a "political myth"? (Sometimes, I am tempted to express this phrase in an even more cynical way...)


Much like the concept of "Bread and Circuses" (Panem et Circenses) in ancient Rome, the elites and the ruling class create illusions of a bright future. Their investments in infrastructure or education are, in essence, just ways to expand the economic pie, keeping the masses from falling into chaos so they will continue to willingly surrender their own labor. They do not (and will never) relinquish their wealth or privileges to save society, because, according to the logic of power, wealth is the very instrument used to maintain dominance. Slogans like "a wealthy populace, a strong nation" or "democracy, fairness, and civilization"—are they not, ultimately, merely the fuel used to feed the power machine of the elite class?


Stripping away the layers of the world's mask like this, I feel as though I am standing at a cognitive crossroads. Realizing this truth does not bring liberation; instead, it seems to bear a much heavier burden of inner turmoil.


Therefore, I wish to bring this dilemma to you: When an intellectual sees through the operational nature of this "matrix," how should they confront it? Faced with that reality, should one choose to see oneself as an "awakened soul" bearing suffering in a fabricated world, or should one accept morphing into a "player," seeking to exploit those exact harsh rules to ascend?


Professor, I listened to your interview with Mr. Gita Wirjawan. I have also re-watched your lectures on the Monad, the "inner fire," and "Plato's Allegory of the Cave" many times. I know, and I internally acknowledge, that I must first realize that "I Matter," that "as long as I follow the guidance of the flame, everything will be alright." Yet, I still constantly agonize over this—there is a world of difference between personal faith and the harsh reality of life.


On one hand, I want to live as an "awakened soul"; I want to be a completely virtuous person, acting purely according to my conscience, and above all, becoming an individual strong enough to "not compete with the world." But on the other hand, I also desire material comfort, Professor. I do not think that if I just let things drift simply without making a breakthrough, I will be able to accumulate enough resources to fulfill my personal ambitions. I fear living a fading, mediocre life. I admit that I, too, have strong personal desires, even the most mundane of cravings, Professor.


I know that sometimes I am truly capable of viewing everything objectively so as not to become angry or compare my life with others. Yet, whenever I sit alone, those "dark thoughts" surface again. Whether it is inferiority, envy, or jealousy toward those "fundamental injustices." That anger is incredibly toxic; it turns my reflections on the "fundamental injustice of natural law" into a heavy anchor dragging me down, stripping away my will to strive. And it is deeply saddening that the more I learn about the world, the smaller I feel, realizing I am utterly powerless to change the situation fundamentally while still maintaining my "sanity."


I eagerly look forward to hearing your enlightening words.


P.S. I sincerely hope that in the future, you will continue to host interactive sessions or 'mid-term exams' like this one. I confess that I usually carry a sense of hesitation and rarely dare to leave a comment, as I never thought I had a chance to be selected. But today, the burning turmoil within has compelled me to write these words to you.

Professor Jiang, you asked us to find holes in your logic. I went through all 133 of your lectures systematically. Here are 5 questions I can't resolve:

1. Your framework is unfalsifiable — and you know it.

In Geo-Strategy END, you said psychohistory can model and predict history. In GT #18, you argue Trump is "deliberately losing" the Iran war. But this is unfalsifiable: if the US wins, Trump is a genius. If the US loses, Trump is ALSO a genius (because he wanted to lose). If neither happens, "it's not time yet." In Geo-Strategy #11, you predict civil war in "10 to 50 years" — a window so wide it can never be proven wrong. Karl Popper would call this pseudoscience: a framework that can explain any outcome predicts nothing.

So my question: **What specific outcome, if it happened, would prove your framework wrong?** Not "I'll adjust the model" — what would BREAK it?

2. Your biggest specific prediction was wrong, and it broke your causal chain.

In Geo-Strategy #5, your central argument was that Trump would pick Nikki Haley as VP, and she would be the one to push for the Iran war. Trump picked JD Vance. This wasn't a minor detail — it was the ENGINE of your Iran prediction. The cause you identified (Haley's hawkish agenda + VP platform) didn't happen, yet the effect you predicted (Iran war) may have happened anyway. If the same outcome occurs through a completely different mechanism than the one you predicted, doesn't that mean your model identified a false cause? You predicted the right destination but drew the wrong map.

3. You hold two "ultimate truths" that contradict each other.

In Secret History and Game Theory, your operating assumption is that the fundamental driver of human behavior is STATUS COMPETITION — everything is a zero-sum game for power positions. But in Great Books #6 and #7, you argue that the deepest insight of Homer, Virgil, and the great poets is that LOVE is the fundamental law of the universe, and the pursuit of power is a violation of that law. Both claims use the word "fundamental." If status competition is the root of everything, then love is just a byproduct. If love is the fundamental law, then status competition is a pathology, not a foundation. Which is it? You can't have two different "bottom layers."

4. Elite overproduction explains everything, therefore it explains nothing.

You use elite overproduction to explain: the Bronze Age Collapse, Maya collapse, the fall of Rome, the French Revolution, the Peloponnesian War, the 2008 financial crisis, and American polarization. When one theory explains EVERY collapse in human history, it has lost all discriminating power. More importantly: where are the counterexamples? Victorian Britain had massive elite surplus (younger sons of aristocrats with no inheritance) — they were channeled to colonies, and Britain thrived. Song Dynasty China had enormous numbers of failed exam candidates — yet Song didn't collapse from internal revolution, it fell to external Mongol invasion. Peter Turchin himself never claimed elite overproduction was the ONLY cause — he uses it as one variable in a four-variable quantitative model. You stripped away the math and kept only the slogan.

5. You critique schools as brainwashing machines — while teaching in one.

You've said: "Schools are designed to brainwash" (SH #1), "Schools are designed to control, not educate" (Civ #54), "Schools teach you not to explore" (Civ #35). But in the same body of work, you celebrate Athenian theater as "the core educational mechanism of democracy," call storytelling "the most powerful educational tool in the world," and praise Humboldt's research university as transformative. And here you are — teaching in a school, asking students to challenge you, posting lectures on YouTube as education. If the DESIGN PURPOSE of schools is control, then your own classroom is either an impossible exception to a universal rule, or the rule isn't universal. Which is it?

Looking forward to Thursday. 期待周四的考试。

That said… I think the framing comes off a bit one-sided,

Listening to this, you’d think the U.S. is uniquely responsible for shaping narratives or using propaganda, when in reality that’s something every major country does to some degree…especially during war, Iran, China, Russia…they all produce messaging that presents their position in the best possible light while downplaying setbacks,

Even with the example of movies like Saving Private Ryan…yes, it’s dramatized…but it’s also loosely rooted in real events, That’s very different from saying it’s just completely made up fantasy used to manipulate people,

So I agree that media can shape how people view war…but I don’t think it’s accurate to frame that as an “American-only” issue, or to imply that other nations aren’t doing the exact same thing,

At the end of the day, a fuller perspective matters…not just one that paints America as the sole driver of propaganda while others are portrayed as if everything is going smoothly,

The real issue isn’t that propaganda exists…it’s that people don’t recognize it when it comes from their own side.

Fascinating theory about the recent operation. Unfortunately, Jiang has missed a few pertinent facts that have colored his analysis a bit:

1) One of the main reasons for this no-man-left-behind mythos, which also ties into the Hollywood thing, is that it encourages bravery and risk taking. The theory behind this is that a pilot who believes he will be rescued is less likely to refuse to follow dangerous orders. Jiang nailed the side effects of this mentality but did not mention this primary intended effect, which is kind of like listing all the side effects of aspirin without mentioning it can help reduce heart attack risk.

2) The Russia-Ukraine war has been going poorly for Ukraine, granted, but it has been going even more poorly for Russia. Everything Jiang has said about Iran having the advantage as a defender applies to Ukraine and then some: like Iran, visible aggression from an external threat cements the resolve of the Ukrainians, but even moreso since Russia has already conducted a genocide against Ukraine (Holodomor), and Russian media has consistently broadcast genocidal messages, so it really is an existential threat to the Ukrainian People rather than just the Ukrainian government; like Iran, Ukraine has developed asymmetric warfare advantages with drone warfare, but even moreso since Ukraine has better technological development and knowledge; like the US, Russia has a distinct logistical challenge in keeping their troops supplied for ongoing military engagements, and notably the logistical challenges for Russia increase over time as Ukraine's ability to strike behind enemy lines increases with the new weapons they develop; and finally, the Ukrainian People live in a society that is more open and meritocratic than the society of their aggressor enemy. Ukraine uses ground drone stretchers to rescue wounded soldiers, then nurses them back to health because they cannot afford to lose soldiers; Russia has consistently used meatwave tactics to trade half a million casualties for a relatively small amount of territory -- their front line has advanced literally slower than a snail -- at their average pace of this war, they will have to sacrifice their entire male population and still not take all of Ukraine. The ultimate outcome of the conflict is still uncertain, but Ukraine is probably going to win since their primary goal is to survive and they have shown a tenacious resolve to survive for the past 4 years.

My questions - 将博士，I've followed your channel for about a year, and deeply appreciate your original mode of analysis and rhetorical pedagogy.

I would like to offer the question you hinted at on Zeteo about the potential for your content to be coopted (for you to become a "useful idiot") by status quo actors. How can this risk be mitigated?

While much of your content includes vital provocations about our inherent sparks of the divine and the emperor's new clothes, I'd like to offer two topics and one frame that I believe would mitigate these risks of cooptation or dillution of your analytic invitations:

Topic 1 - Stronger analysis of global antagonists - How might you double down on your strongest explanatory argumentation, the real and continually obscured role of secret societies? What sources might bolster your exposition of conspiracy & secret societies? Have you explored the 2018 academic work Occult Features of Anarchism by anthropologist Erica Lagalisse (which I think builds nicely on your analysis of Newton's eschatology, and traces the various impacts of secret societies, sometimes against the status quo), or Michael Parenti's Conspiracy and Class Power (rich in arguments and historical references of how power seeks to discredit & censor)?

Topic 2 - Stronger analysis of global protagonists - How might you enrich your critical assessments of status quo actors with countervailing examples? While I appreciate your background in Western classics, how might drawing from situated, non-Western cosmologies provide examples for students to compare approaches and worldviews, such as the text The 11 Pictures of Time (Dr CK Raju's refutation of Hawking's brief history of time -- another source that traces Newton's zionism to modern secularism/scientism),  Decolonizing The Mind by Ngiguwa Thiong'o, Pedagogy of the Oppressed, Land as Pedagogy, etc.

Frame 3 - Pedagogical diversity - How might explicit personal open-ended inquiry throughout your lectures deepen comprehension and enable students more analogies for critical reflection? As a polemic against the current status quo, your standard lecture format is certainly potent, but the questions asked by students at the end of class in the dozens I've viewed seem to predictably remain focused on the global antagonists you narrate, which risks insights remaining abstract. How might presenting a stronger analysis of the history of conspiracy (including the hidden/erased conspiracies of the people) and alternatives to Western modes of thought/organization enable more listeners and students to make connections/insights to their local contexts, especially if you present stories of communities impacted by and responding collectively to these news events, with opportunities throughout the class to personally reflect on the emotions raised by these topics. For instance, how might inviting students to think about recent community responses to ICE in Minneapolis lay the foundation for a fuller conception of US domestic conflict?

Question for Prof Jiang, delivered with respect and desire for greater understanding:

To what extent do you problematise game theory, in its capability as a theoreteical lens for analysing Middle Eastern geopolitics? Is it possible that game theory's assumption of the individual entity acting in its own self-interest, is, to an extent, at odds with the prevailing Islamic creed of that region, which holds as a central tenet that, "No man is a true believer until he loves for his brother what he loves for himself"? I am not suggesting pure altruism is at play; rather, I wonder if some form of genuine camaraderie, such as that expressed by the Houthis and even some Sunni groups, is a sign of a willingness to make some sacrifices for 'the other'.

This is not to discard game theory's applicability to West Asian geopolitics. Rather, it is borne of wondering whether inviting other theoretical lenses into the conversation - and perhaps the way that actors like Iran et al describe their motivations could be a starting point for finding these additional lenses - might strengthen your already strong analytical framework. Hi Jiang. I'm an avid student of your classes from Brazil. This is the first time I'll have to disagree with you.

At 38:00, when you talk about the examples Hollywood brings to the public to fabricate a propagandized version of the military, Black Hawk Down doesn't really do that. Reading the book, we can confirm the movie is very grounded in the reality of the events, with a few exceptions: the character of Hoot, who is supposed to represent a multitude of Delta Force operators in Gothic Serpent along with this mythological view of them as "invincible," and the way Matt Eversmann was misplaced in the chain of events to become a character the audience follows throughout the movie. Eversmann was in the lost convoy in Mogadishu and did not spend the night waiting for the next convoy to be rescued as shown. And as a matter of fact, Michael Durant, the pilot of the UH-60 that went down in Somalia, was never rescued in the movie at all.

I think the perfect example you should have brought up of how Hollywood pulls propaganda stunts on failed military actions is Lone Survivor and Operation Red Wings. There are plenty of resources around the internet questioning how the movie and subsequently the book were a fabricated story to cover how special forces (Navy SEALs in that case) were actually ambushed and killed without much chance of a real fight during their reconnaissance mission. The operation was such a fiasco that it got even worse when the rescue helicopter was downed by RPG fire killing in total 19 special forces members and losing 1 Chinook helicopter. The movie, of course, tries to dress all of this up as a heroic survival attempt as this was a MAJOR propaganda stunt by the Afghan insurgents at the time (there are videos of them posing with the captured equipment from the team including their M4 rifles, a Toughbook laptop with a keycard that granted access to blueprints of some US embassy and other sensitive material).

Cheers from Brazil and thank you for your lessons.
